observations.text: SP, due to a mission planning flow that stopped at the route legs, did not select emergency airfields for the low-level segment and did not plan heading, time and fuel from every turning point to the nearest emergency airfield. The aeronautical charts were left unmarked for the diversion routing, with the result that the IP directed the selection and worked part of the diversion planning in the cockpit. Emergency airfield planning could not be completed without assistance.

SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, did not extract the applicable figures from the A/C performance charts of the Check List before the navigation sortie. Range and fuel figures for the planned profile were therefore not available in flight, with the result that the IP provided the values and directed the fuel checks at the turning points. Use of the Check List performance charts was not achieved without assistance.

SP planned and flew the navigation sortie within the standards desired for this Training Section, selecting emergency airfields and using the aeronautical charts after the IP's verbal prompts. Heading, time and fuel to the nearest emergency airfield were then computed correctly at each turning point, although recognition of the need to update the plan came with delay on two occasions. Marginal performance for the Training Section - independent recognition of the update points is expected to improve.

SP selected emergency airfields for each leg and planned heading, time and fuel to the nearest emergency airfield without the IP's prompts. Minor errors in reading the A/C performance charts of the Check List were recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention. Task prioritization in the cockpit remained ordered throughout the route. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP exercised accurate and timely airmanship throughout the navigation sortie, choosing emergency airfields correctly and planning heading, time and fuel to the nearest one from every turning point without assistance. Use of the aeronautical charts and of the A/C performance charts from the Check List was proficient, and as a wingman SP anticipated No1's intentions without assuming them. Judgment and flight discipline were maintained under the workload of the low-level segment. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP displayed exceptional airmanship for this stage of training, holding position, fuel state and terrain clearance in a single updated picture while planning correctly the diversion to the nearest emergency airfield from every turning point. The A/C performance charts from the Check List and the aeronautical charts were used with precision above the desired level, and spare capacity remained available for lookout and formation duties. As a wingman SP anticipated No1's intentions and confirmed every change before acting, never assuming. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an unstructured chart preparation that left the diversion data off the map, did not have heading, time and fuel to the nearest emergency airfield available at the turning points of the route. The fix against the aeronautical chart was lost after the second turning point, with the result that the IP navigated part of the leg and directed the recovery to track. The airmanship requirements of the sortie could not be met without assistance.

SP, due to lack of awareness of the fuel state during the working phase of the sortie, did not reassess the fuel required to reach the nearest emergency airfield as the route progressed. The decision to continue was taken without reference to the A/C performance charts of the Check List, with the result that the IP directed both the fuel check and the diversion decision. Risk management and judgment required IP direction over the second half of the route.

SP, due to a chart handling technique that occupied both hands and interrupted the outside scan, did not keep a continuous fix on position against the aeronautical chart during the low-level legs. Emergency airfield data were recomputed at two turning points only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result that the plan trailed the aircraft. Errors were recognized and corrected with delay.

SP, due to retention of the briefed mental model after the actual route had changed, assumed No1's intentions at the re-route instead of confirming them. The new turning point and the associated emergency airfield data were not updated, with the result that the correct plan was re-established only after the IP's verbal prompts. Recognition of the changed situation was delayed.

SP met the airmanship requirements of the navigation sortie within the desired standards, selecting emergency airfields and planning heading, time and fuel to the nearest one with minor errors that were self-corrected in a timely manner. Chart work at two turning points was completed late and reduced the time available for lookout, without requiring IP's intervention. Marginal performance for the Training Section - consistency in chart discipline at the turning points is expected to improve.

SP kept an accurate picture of position, fuel state and terrain throughout the route and planned heading, time and fuel to the nearest emergency airfield from every turning point without error. The A/C performance charts from the Check List and the aeronautical charts were used quickly and correctly, and no IP prompt was required at any point of the sortie. As a wingman SP anticipated No1's intentions and confirmed them before acting. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP demonstrated exceptional airmanship for this Training Section, prioritizing tasks so that navigation, fuel management and lookout were all serviced without saturation. Emergency airfield selection and the associated heading, time and fuel figures were correct at every turning point and were revised without prompting when the weather forced a re-route. Judgment and flight discipline remained above the level desired for this stage of training. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a cockpit workflow that placed all chart work inside the turns, did not keep the navigation plan and the emergency airfield data current along the route. Neither the diversion heading nor the fuel required to the nearest emergency airfield was available when the weather deteriorated, with the result that the IP took the diversion decision and flew part of the recovery. Planning and execution of the diversion could not be completed without assistance.

SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the navigation computation at the expense of the outside scan, did not maintain awareness of terrain clearance and of the formation position during the low-level leg. The judgment to abandon the computation and fly the aircraft first was not exercised, with the result that the IP took control to re-establish terrain and lateral separation. Task prioritization under saturation requires further work.

SP, due to an unsystematic sequence in using the A/C performance charts from the Check List, did not derive the fuel figure for the diversion leg at the required turning point. The emergency airfield chosen was appropriate, but heading and time to it were computed only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result that the plan trailed the aircraft by one leg. Errors were recognized and corrected with delay.

SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the planned route after the information that invalidated it had already been received, did not re-evaluate the nearest emergency airfield when the destination weather was passed as below minima. The alternative plan was formed only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result that the diversion was commenced later than the computed fuel figures supported. Recognition of the decision point was delayed.

SP, due to a chart folding technique that hid the adjacent sector during the second leg, did not identify the alternative emergency airfield at the first attempt after the re-route. The correct airfield and the associated heading, time and fuel were established shortly afterwards, with the result of a minor delay in the plan, recognized and corrected in a timely manner without IP's intervention.

SP, due to distraction by a secondary cockpit task at the turning point, did not complete the fuel check against the planned figure at the briefed time. The check was carried out one minute later on SP's own initiative and confirmed the reserve to the nearest emergency airfield, with the result of a minor deviation from the planned sequence, corrected without IP's intervention. As a wingman SP continued to anticipate No1's intentions without assuming them.

SP exercised accurate and timely airmanship throughout the navigation sortie, choosing emergency airfields correctly and planning heading, time and fuel to the nearest one from every turning point without IP's intervention. Use of the aeronautical charts and of the A/C performance charts from the Check List was correct, although the workload of the final leg left little spare capacity for lookout. Marginal performance for the Training Section - capacity available for lookout and formation duties is expected to improve.

SP demonstrated exceptional airmanship for the navigation phase, keeping position, fuel state, weather and terrain consolidated in one picture that was updated at every turning point. Emergency airfield selection and the associated heading, time and fuel figures were faultless, the A/C performance charts from the Check List were applied without hesitation, and spare capacity remained for lookout and radio work. As a wingman SP anticipated No1's intentions but confirmed every change before acting, and flight discipline was maintained without exception. Above end of block MIF achieved.
